content: Welcome back! In this video, I kind of decided to do this on the spur of the moment, in large part because it's a concept I've been really trying to piece together. I want to get my thoughts all out there to conceptualize this theory that we're going to get into, which basically summarizes how to plan out top set progression within a training block. In a lot of my other videos, I really go much more in depth into the actual programming of top sets, backoffs, weekly structure, and block structure. So if you're wanting to know more about that, I have plenty of videos that delve deeply into that topic. But for this video, what I really want to look at is understanding, choosing loading, and planning progression week to week. Sure, if you're an athlete or a coach, you may have seen where someone has started out a block. Because of the way they started out—whether they just came out of the gate too hot, chose a load that they thought would be the correct RPE and it was an overshoot, or maybe they just felt really good and they did some weight that was even more than they expected at the allotted RPE—we see as the block progresses, they start to fizzle out because of those earlier week load selections. There's an understanding of why we need to progress and plan out at a certain rate through a training block to optimally end our block where we want to. To understand this concept, there are two kinds of...

Theories and principles we need to understand that guide this process and way of thinking are one, the repeated bout effect, and two, understanding of adaptation preceding overload. So, one, the repeated bout effect, basically just states, in summary, that when we provide a certain stimulus, as we have exposures, we start to adapt to it and we get better. I mean, a really good example that people can pick up pretty easily is if, all of a sudden, out of nowhere, I give you sets of eight. The first week feels really crappy; sometimes it feels like you're exhausted. The second week feels better, and then by the third week, you're likely even moving weight faster than you did in week one, and now it's feeling easy. That's the repeated bout effect, which leads into adaptation. Adaptation precedes overload. The repeated bout effect is that adaptation period to a new stimulus. When we are thinking about block structure, and when we're considering progression in powerlifting, we have to understand that adaptation to the stimulus precedes overloading the stimulus. That's why we usually have a progressive— not always linear, but a progressive model in a block where weight starts to get heavier. Whether we actually have ascending plans like RPE, or even people have a static plan of RPE, we see something over a block start to get heavier because as we adapt to the stimulus, we then gain the ability to overload. That structure, and what really differs between individuals, is that adaptation time period and the length that the repeated overload effect adaptation takes, and the effect of where they start a block versus where they end the block. Your training max is not the same, or your actual one RM training max, whatever it may be, is not the same every day, nor is it the same week one versus week four. Yet, people tend to treat it the same, and they start this overload process from week one versus allowing the adaptation and knowing how to plan the block accordingly. This should be based not only on actual lifting data but also on the analytical process of looking at the percentages and the increases that you see weekly. Being able to tailor your actual plan progressions based off of that. So, with that, in this video, it's going to be a lot of just me talking and screen sharing to kind of conceptualize and show what I mean by planning weekly top set progression based off of actual data, data, and analytics. So, we're going to be looking at static versus variable training maxes and how they dictate block progression. We're going to be looking at different scenarios of block progression. We're going to look at, based off of this information, how an athlete can plan that progression accordingly. And then lastly, we'll look at how an athlete or coach can basically take past data and customize ranges of a week and/or weekly plan progressions based on past data. Data all right! So, without further ado, let's get right on into it. With this setup, we're going to have some static things. This person we're going to be using for the squat has a 200-kilo squat, which is 440 pounds. They're going to be doing a top set of five, and that's just going to be the same throughout. We’re also going to have a progression model from week one to week four of five RPEs: six, seven, and eight. That doesn't mean that's the best one. Again, in a lot of other videos, I talk about the reasons behind top set progress—the why behind top set progression and loading—and trying to figure that out. This is just for the example of what we're trying to conceptualize here. So, the issue with just a model of thinking is I can do the... The same every week is that if we were to do, let's say, eight RPE at 162.5 kilos on week four, and since the progression model is correct, that is going to likely be our strongest week and that is going to be our highest estimated 1rm. The mistake a lot of people make is they come back around to week one expecting the same performance. So, let's get into some different examples of how that plays out. If it was a perfect world, everyone could be able to maintain the same exact strength every single week. If this person was doing one by five at five RPE in week one, they could handle, based off of just generalized percentages, which I have shown before, but here's my general RPE chart, they could be able to do 147.5 kilos. From there, it's about a three percent jump weekly. You can see here, if I'm doing, like, we'll just use this for example, like, uh, four reps to five reps, six up every rep, to an extent, on average for most people, is about three percent. Again, in some other videos, I talked about differing factors there, in particular, the distance traveled video, of where that's going to change. But this is just a general concept that we're going to work on; that it's a three percent jump weekly to either one, go between an RPE, you can see here, 9.2, 9.2 to 89.2, or between reps. So, it's about three percent. You would expect if strength stayed static, they could jump five kilos a week and/or three percent. The issue is, this isn't likely going to happen for multiple. There are reasons: one, we're going to see strength fluctuations week to week; but two, if your week one is as strong as week four, that would be an outlier. I'm not saying it can't happen, but it would be an outlier that likely isn't occurring for most people. So, there's a good chance if you're taking the weight you lifted on week four and then reapplying it to what you did in week one, this is no longer going to be a 5 RPE. So, what is likely going to happen is if this person has that static training max thought process but forces progression, they're going to do that 147.5 at a 5 RPE, thinking it's going to be a 5 RPE, and it's more likely they are now trying to overload before they allow the adaptations to occur, likely because either week one... It is coming off of a deload, so there's some slight detraining. And if they're wave loading, there's still a period of fatigue that is waiting to dissipate. By having some lower load training and an intensity drop in those earlier weeks, we can ramp back up. So, what we very likely might see is that they do 147 and a half at a 5 RPE. It's not a 5 RPE; it's more like a 6.

So, the next week they jump up, and instead of being able to do 152 and a half, they can only do 150. Then the next week they do 155, and then the following week they do 160, all of the correct RPEs. Again, this isn't set in stone; not everyone's going to happen like this. I'm not saying if you slightly overshoot week one, all of a sudden the rest of your block is messed up, but just the general theory and concept here. The overshoot in week one and trying to match the static training max is then going to basically affect the remainder of the training block and slightly mute top-end strength, leading to a slight underperformance. There is also the option, though, that some people come off of a deload or a wave-loading structure and feel really, really good in week one. They might even decide, 'I actually feel stronger,' and you can see here that this person is actually able to do 150 kilos at a 5 RPE. They actually did it! Awesome! But what I see way too often—and honestly, this is where I started conceptualizing this—is that week one goes really well, and then everything kind of... Of sputters from there, they had this highest estimated one RM in week one. Then we see, okay, maybe they kind of matched at weeks two and three. But then by week four, they just kind of sputter out because of this exposure length that we have in this block length. That we have, that tends to work. We kind of came out of the gate too hot. Even though it matched the RPE, it was still a load that was pushing us to a percentage and an estimated one RM that we weren't even matching the prior block on week four. So we start to be a little bit muted on our strength, and we get a little bit more beat up and fatigued, and we kind of sputter out early in the block. We almost kind of peaked in weeks one, two, and three, and then we sputter out on week four versus high performing. Week one, and you allow progression knowing that you tend to get beat up from going too early and too quickly in a block. So, in reality, you might actually choose to undershoot a touch and keep things conservative. Even though it's a 5 RPE, RPE is a range; it doesn't mean you have to do 5 RPE. We're going to get to kind of the athlete planning aspect of this because here's the thing: if you believe that 147.5 is the right load, you would also have to believe that you are just as strong as your best, which is that most 200-kilo training max. But if you're not this person, let's say they actually did a 5 RPE, but their training max on this day was 192. Well, the correct load progression was 142.5. Now, you don't know what your estimated 1rm is, but we're going to get to how we can kind of understand and plan that. This person, though, has an understanding that in weeks one and two, they're likely not going to be as strong as in weeks three and four. So, they choose lower load progressions; they do 142.5, and it's around a 5 RPE. They do 150; maybe it's even a little bit under a 6 RPE. But they know that as they progress into week three, they're actually now going to be close to where their actual top-end strength is. They're going to hit that 157, which is planned. But since they left a little in the tank and they were able to be better with load selection earlier in the block, they now have a little extra in week four to be able to push and likely hit some type. Of ability for pr or rep pr, and you can see the estimated 1rm is 202.5. So the overriding key here is that we have to understand that our actual strength is variable. If our goal is to be the strongest in weeks three and four, we're likely not going to be our strongest in weeks one and two. We need to notate that even though week four states that we should do 147, there is a very good chance 147 is going to be higher than a 5 RPE in week one. Therefore, we need to have an understanding of the variable training max that’s going to occur throughout a training block, and how we're likely going to be a touch weaker in week one, and we're likely going to get stronger as the block progresses. So in this model, we're allowing for... progression, um, and then the same thing goes for another example. Some people underperform in week one, so I use the example that they were high performing. They came out of the gate and they actually felt really good. Even though 150 felt like a five RPE, they kind of went too fast, and then it sputtered through the block versus allowing them to be able to kind of progress through the block, knowing that we need to save some in the tank for week four. Underperforming means they do not feel strong in week one, and they try to force the progression anyway, which goes a lot back to that kind of static mode where they're just going to choose the load based on what they did the prior week, and they're going to force it. But then that's going to be too heavy and likely overshoot. It's going to kind of sputter them out, and they're not going to be able to load progress. Versus, again, underperforming, this is probably the more likely scenario for most. They're not going to be as strong on week one; they're going to know that their estimated one-rep max is going to be lower because they are not meant to be as strong on week one. So, they are going to have to adjust their load selection based off of that and likely have bigger jumps throughout the block. This is one of the keys here, and we're going to get to how I break this out. If we were having a static training load and we want to jump one RPE every week, that...

It would be about a three percent increase. But what is our actual strength in week one versus week two? If there is a gap of, let's say, four to six percent difference, well, that could be managed. And so you can see here, instead of three percent, it's five percent. So we're actually adding; we're basically saying that we are six percent weaker in week one to week four. Through those weeks, we start to gather and adapt so that we can then overload and reach that maximal strength level, and actually have that output. But we need to plan for the fact that we need to make up that six percent gap throughout the training block. And so what I mean by that, and to kind of actually show the percentages here, maybe you should actually track estimated one around. I do that with some people. I mean, I honestly, at this point as a coach, can kind of just know. I don't really actually track it like actual data-wise; I can kind of just tell and individualize from there. But if it's something that would help you, you can actually track it, and it doesn't mean the estimated 1rm is accurate. They rarely are ever very accurate, but the actual changes week to week could be accurate depending on someone's ability to rate RPE. So here's the example: let's say that, uh, this is our estimated training max on week one. Based off of our top, like, this is our estimated one RM off of our top set. It's 192.5. Week two is 195, week three is 197.5, week four is 200. We have basically about a two and a half kilo. Jump each week on our estimated one RM based off of our top sets, and the performance there. You can see that's about a 1.3 percent increase week to week and in total about 3.85 percent. So if you normally have nine percent, that's the three percent jump week to week, totaling up. Well, if our actual training max is changing by 3.85 percent from week one to week four, that's actually nine percent plus 3.85 percent, and let's get this to twelve point percent from week one to week four, not nine percent. So the load progression needs to basically follow that pattern, and that's something if we can actually see that pattern, we can then actually plan for it. I'm not saying like all of a sudden immediately go out. And start changing everything. But if you start to see this pattern, you could then start basically planning load progression and top set progression, knowing that, okay, if I am jumping one RPE each week for four weeks or for three weeks, after week one, that's nine percent. And if, on average, my estimated one-rep max jumps 3.85 percent throughout a block, that means my load progression needs to be about 12.8 percent from week one to week four, not nine percent. If we do nine percent, we are then likely going too heavy on week one. So, what does this mean for the athlete? I'm going to use the example of the athlete that tends to set a goal for themselves at the end of the block. I would say, especially with RPE-based training, an athlete gets their... I'm using a new training block myself. For example, I send them their 4-week training block, and they see the ranges. They see what they've done before and they say, "Okay, I hit 162.5 last time I did sets of five; my goal was 165." They already kind of have that in their head, and that's not a bad thing. I like that they set goals for themselves. But then, how can we plan backwards from there? As an athlete, if you were to plan backwards from a static training max model, you would think, "Okay, if I want to hit 165, that means I need to hit 160 in week 3, 155 in week 2, and then 150 in week 1." There's multiple things wrong there. One, you're planning 165 to be an increase over your current e1rm of 200. Again, these are all just numbers; they're just... Conceptualizing it, but if your current e1rm is 200, you are planning to be higher than that. So, not only are you planning a static model, you're also planning this low progression to be heavier than you've ever done before. You're starting out over your actual e1rm normally, and then you're trying to maintain that throughout the block. That's what I see way too often: people try to say, "Okay, I want to hit this pr at the end of the block; here's how I get there." They plan off of a higher e1rm than they've ever been at, and they plan off a static load or a static training max. This means that they're going to act like or believe that their training max is 202.5 every single week, so you can see the load progression.

From week 1 to week 4, there is a 15-kilo difference, and the difference is about 10 percent. Instead, what they should do is likely plan out based off of a variable training max. That's where you have to kind of understand the general progression block and knowing where you start week one versus week four. So, what this athlete could do, and then this model of 5 RPE, 6 RPE, 7 RPE—if their goal is 165—here's how I can plan my loading. Okay, so I'm going to start out. This goes back to the 3.85 percent, so if I know that I am going to have a 3.585 increase from week one to week four and my goal is to squat 165 for a set of five, here are the actual jumps you should be taking: 145 in week 1, 150 in week 2, 157.5 in week 3, and then 165. And you can see that the variable increased the training max, and you can see how now it's no longer a 10% jump from week 1 to week 4. It is a 13.8% jump. So, they have now planned to be able to load progress not only based off of the RPE going up but the general data and concept that they are going to gain 3.85% of strength from week one to week four based on past training data. Key there: past training data. Just don't take this number as verbatim; you need to know kind of what you're doing from week one through week four to have an understanding. There are a multitude of variables that go into why we see that increase from week one to week four. Some of it's physiological in the sense of the adaptation, the overload, and the repeated bouts. The middle ground that I expect is 162.5, so I give a range five kilos above or below, 157 to 167.5, to give the athlete a guiding factor. I think, overwhelmingly, ranges are better than just giving a straight RPE because it helps provide a guiding factor and keeps people accountable, like a ground of where they are. See, things tend to sputter later in the block, and so this is where we're about kind of controlling that top-set progression to know, like, take the wins early in the block. If we slightly undershoot, that's awesome; we know we have now more room to grow as the block progresses. So maybe this athlete's going to go 145 and then 150, and then I'm going to say as we progress into the block, we can start pushing a little bit more if you're... Feeling really good! Maybe push a little bit higher to the top end on week three, so they go with 57, and then by week four they go to 165. So, we kind of loaded up that progression later in the block when it's time to overload, and we kept things more conservative earlier in the block when we needed to adapt. So, that is the conceptual theory of how to plan weekly top set progression. Again, this is not set in stone; do not take these exact numbers and apply them to yourself. But the theory here is that we need to have an understanding of our load progression based off of a variable training max and our general strength increase throughout a block. That's something where, as an athlete and a coach, you can track over time and try to get an idea. Of that general progression, or as a coach, you can just kind of have an idea that I'm going to start out my lifter a little bit more conservative, so that we have more room to build throughout the block. Knowing that week one and week two, we do not plan for them to be at their near maximal strength, we want that to build the adaptation so that we can then overload as we get to the end of our training block.
